from.place: Integral exceptional-adjoint proof, paragraph 2, displayed derived coefficient-adjunction and inverse-limit calculation; technical foundations for the finite-adjunction-diagram realization, specifically the full functor-category pushout comparison in lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization. Technical input: Cartesian simplicial model of marked simplicial sets over a point. Foundational sublemma: Marked-anodyne lifting, products and mapping objects.

title: Marked-anodyne lifting, products and mapping objects
statement:
Use the universes and simplicial sets of [def-weil-size-convention] and [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A marked simplicial set is $(X,M)$ with $M\subseteq X_1$ containing all degenerate edges; morphisms preserve $M$, and product markings are coordinatewise. Write $K^ lat,K^\sharp$ for minimal and full markings, and $C^
atural$ for equivalences marked in a quasicategory. Write $\operatorname{Map}^\epsilon(X,Y)_n=\operatorname{Hom}(X	imes(\Delta^n)^\epsilon,Y)$ for $\epsilon= lat,\sharp$. The marked-anodyne maps form the closure under pushouts, transfinite compositions and retracts of: (i) $(\Lambda_i^n)^ lat\hookrightarrow(\Delta^n)^ lat$ for $0<i<n$; (ii) $(\Lambda_n^n,E\cap(\Lambda_n^n)_1)\hookrightarrow(\Delta^n,E)$ for $n>0$, where $E$ consists of degenerate edges and the final edge; (iii) $(\Lambda_1^2)^\sharp\amalg_{(\Lambda_1^2)^ lat}(\Delta^2)^ lat\hookrightarrow(\Delta^2)^\sharp$; (iv) $K^ lat	o K^\sharp$ for Kan complexes $K$. A right lifting property means existence of a diagonal in every commutative square against the specified maps.

This class is generated by a small set: in (iv) countable Kan complexes suffice. Every marked simplicial set has a functorial marked-anodyne map to some $C^
atural$. A marked simplicial set has the right lifting property against this class to the terminal marked point if and only if it is $C^
atural$ for a quasicategory $C$. The pushout product $i\mathbin\square j$ of a marked-anodyne map $i$ with a degreewise injective marked map $j$ is marked anodyne; here the pushout product of $A	o B$ and $U	o V$ is $(B	imes U)\amalg_{A	imes U}(A	imes V)	o B	imes V$. For any $X,C$, $\operatorname{Map}^ lat(X,C^
atural)$ is a quasicategory and $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,C^
atural)$ is its core and is Kan. Restriction along any degreewise injective marked map is a Kan fibration on $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(-,C^
atural)$; it is a trivial Kan fibration when that map is marked anodyne. The same restriction is a trivial Kan fibration if the map is $A^ lat	o A$ described next: the underlying simplicial set $A$ is the quotient of $\Delta^3$ representing pairs $(\sigma,e)$ with $d_1\sigma=s_0e$, $d_2\sigma=s_1e$, and its marking adds to the degenerate edges the image of $\Delta^{\{0,1\}}$. In fact this last restriction is an isomorphism. All assertions are universe-relative and the marked-anodyne replacement stays in the input universe.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1; Remark 3.1.1.3; Proposition 3.1.1.6 and Remark 3.1.1.10 (point case); Proposition 3.1.2.3; Remark 3.1.3.1; Remark 3.1.3.4; Lemma 3.1.3.6; proof of Proposition 3.1.3.7(1) for the finite equivalence detector A. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived. No Stacks tag states this simplicial homotopy-theoretic result.

proof.text: First identify the objects having the asserted lifting property. Lifting against (i) says exactly that the underlying simplicial set $C$ is a quasicategory. For any marked edge $e$, lifting (ii) for every $n\geq2$ says that all final outer horns ending in $e$ fill. The converse clause of [lem-cbc-equivalence-outer-horn-filling] makes $e$ an equivalence. On the other hand the core $C^\simeq$ is Kan by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. The map $(C^\simeq)^\flat\to(C^\simeq)^\sharp$ of type (iv), with its underlying inclusion into $C$, forces every equivalence edge to be marked. Therefore the markings are exactly the equivalences. Conversely, $C^\natural$ lifts (i) by the quasicategory condition and (ii) for $n\geq2$ by the same outer-horn lemma. For $n=1$ use the degenerate edge at the specified vertex. It lifts (iii) because the third edge of a triangle represents the composite of the two consecutive edges; if the consecutive edges are $a,b$, its inverse is represented by $a^{-1}b^{-1}$, with the two inverse equations following by the cited associativity and identity homotopies. The associative composition and inverse homotopies here are the conclusion of [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine]. Finally every edge of a Kan complex is an equivalence by the converse outer-horn criterion already cited (all its outer horns fill). A simplicial map from a Kan complex therefore preserves equivalences: inverse-triangle witnesses map to inverse-triangle witnesses. It therefore lifts (iv). A lifting property extends from generators to pushouts by the pushout universal property, to a transfinite composite by successive extensions and the colimit universal property, and to a retract by inclusion and projection of squares.

source.place: Definition 3.1.1.1; point-case proof of Proposition 3.1.1.6; equivalence outer-horn criterion Proposition 1.2.4.3.

proof.text: For any edge in a Kan complex $K$, begin with the simplicial subset generated by that edge. Repeatedly adjoin, for every horn in the current subset, one filler chosen in $K$ and all its faces and degeneracies. There are only countably many such horns at each stage; after countably many stages the union is a countable Kan subcomplex containing the edge, since each finite horn occurs at some stage. Well-order the edges of $K$. At each stage push out $L^\flat\to L^\sharp$ for a countable Kan subcomplex $L$ containing the next edge, mapping its minimally marked domain into the underlying $K$ with its current markings. The underlying simplicial set stays $K$, and the markings become their union with the edges of $L$. The final marking is all of $K_1$. This expresses (iv) using only countable Kan complexes, and proves the small-generation assertion. Countable simplicial sets and their markings have a set of representatives in the fixed universe.

source.place: Remark 3.1.1.3; explicit countable-horn-filler and marking-attachment argument.

proof.text: Small limits and colimits of marked sets have underlying degreewise limits and colimits: the limit marking is tested by every projection, and the colimit marking consists of images of marked edges. These formulas satisfy the universal properties by testing edges. Apply [lem-coef-small-object-cell-factorization] to the small generating set $J$ from Step 2 and the terminal map of each marked set $X$. Its domains are countable. Take $\kappa=\aleph_1$: a map from a countable domain into an $\aleph_1$-chain of marked monomorphisms factors through one stage, since its countably many simplices and marked-edge conditions occur below a common bound; equality is detected in the same manner. The hypothesis of the cited factorization theorem is thus satisfied. It gives functorially $X\to Q\to*$ with first map a $J$-cell map and second map $J$-injective. A coproduct of $J$-maps can be serialized by well-ordering its summands, so the first map is marked anodyne. Step 1 identifies $Q=C^\natural$. This construction and its colimits use only sets in the input universe.

source.place: Remark 3.1.1.3 and the universe-relative small-object argument of Proposition A.1.2.5.

proof.text: Put $e:\{1\}^\sharp\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$ and $b_m:(\partial\Delta^m)^\flat\to(\Delta^m)^\flat$. The three saturated classes in [lem-coef-marked-endpoint-prism-generation] are equal, with its $I$ exactly our family (i) and its $F$ exactly our family (ii). Consequently replacing family (ii) by the endpoint prisms $P(\partial\Delta^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m)=e\square b_m$ leaves the marked-anodyne class unchanged after adjoining the same families (iii),(iv) on both sides. The final assertion of that lemma also gives $e\square h^\flat$ marked anodyne for every underlying simplicial monomorphism $h$. This is the precise endpoint-prism input used below; the marked equality of saturated classes, rather than an unmarked retraction alone, is needed here.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.1.5, applied to the marked families in the item.

proof.text: Here are the two saturation reductions, in the marked category itself. For a degreewise injective marked map, apply [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells] to its underlying simplicial monomorphism: adjoining the missing nondegenerate simplices in increasing dimension gives the boundary attachments $b_m$. Give each new simplex only its degenerate markings; the pushout retains all markings already present. After this underlying simplicial filtration, add each remaining target marking with $a:(\Delta^1)^\flat\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$. When a simplex is attached retain only the old markings; all additional markings are added in the second stage. In each fixed variable the pushout product preserves pushouts and retracts; a continuous chain of attachments in that variable induces the chain of pushout products, whose successive relative maps are pushouts of the corresponding products of attachments. These assertions follow by distributing products over degreewise colimits; on markings both sides mark exactly the images of pairs of marked edges. A coproduct of attachments is handled by well-ordering its summands. Thus it suffices to check $i\square j$ on the four families (i), endpoint prisms, (iii), (iv), and $j=b_m,a$. No assertion about saturation of unmarked sets is substituted for this marked argument.

source.place: Reduction in the proof of Proposition 3.1.2.3; degreewise colimit and marking argument.

proof.text: For the inner-horn cases (A1),(A2), first use [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product]: the underlying product with $b_m$ is inner anodyne. The horn inclusion has the required left lifting property by the definition of inner fibration. By [lem-coef-inner-horn-cell-generation], this product is a retract of a small inner-horn cell map. Minimal marking preserves its coproducts, pushouts and continuous unions: their only marked edges are images of degenerate edges, hence exactly the degeneracies of the underlying colimit. It also preserves retract diagrams. Thus the minimally marked product lies in the closure of (i). For the product with $a$, the underlying map is an identity, and every newly marked vertical edge already comes from the source horn, which contains every vertex of the simplex. This product is an isomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.2.3, cases (A1),(A2); Remark 3.1.1.4. The cellular comparison is the cited existing Mathlib leaf.

proof.text: For the endpoint-prism cases (B1),(B2), the product $(e\square b_n)\square b_m$ is $e\square(b_n\square b_m)$, by permuting product coordinates and identifying the union of the three source pieces. The map $b_n\square b_m$ is the inclusion $(\partial\Delta^n\times\Delta^m)\cup(\Delta^n\times\partial\Delta^m)\subseteq\Delta^n\times\Delta^m$, hence a simplicial monomorphism. The final assertion of [lem-coef-marked-endpoint-prism-generation] applies. For $(e\square b_n)\square a$, if $n>0$, the boundary contains every vertex, so every new vertical marking is already present and the map is an isomorphism. If $n=0$, the source marks the two vertical edges and the upper horizontal edge of the square. Its upper triangle marks the diagonal by (iii); its lower triangle then has the diagonal and final vertical edge marked, so [lem-coef-marked-triangle-cancellation] marks the lower horizontal edge. These are pushouts of the indicated marking extensions.

For the triangle-generator cases (C1),(C2), the product of (iii) with $b_m$ has identity underlying map. If $m>0$, its boundary piece already marks every pair $(h,s_0v)$, since each vertex $v$ of $\Delta^m$ is in the boundary; these are exactly the target markings. For $m=0$ the product is (iii) itself. For the product of (iii) with $a$, direct inspection of coordinatewise markings leaves just the edge $([0,2],[0,1])$ unmarked. The triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(2,1)$ has both consecutive edges already marked. Pushing out (iii) along this triangle marks exactly the missing diagonal.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.2.3, cases (C1),(C2); explicit coordinatewise marking checks.

proof.text: For the Kan-marking cases (D1),(D2), the product of (iv) with $b_m$ has identity underlying map. If $m>0$, every target marked edge is $(h,s_0v)$, and is already marked by the boundary piece because $v\in\partial\Delta^m$. For $m=0$ the product is (iv). For the product with $a$, the underlying object is $K\times\Delta^1$; its source marks exactly the edges with at least one degenerate coordinate. For each missing edge $(h,[0,1])$, take the triangle $(s_1h,(0,0,1))$ with vertices $(d_1h,0),(d_0h,0),(d_0h,1)$. Both consecutive edges are already marked, and its diagonal is the desired edge. A pushout of (iii) marks this edge; a small well-ordered composite does so for all missing edges. Thus all eight generating products have now been checked. The saturation reduction in Step 5 proves the full pushout-product assertion, including maps adding only markings.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.2.3, cases (D1),(D2); explicit degeneracy triangle attachments.

proof.text: For arbitrary marked $X$, $\operatorname{Map}^\flat(X,C^\natural)$ is the full simplicial subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(X,C)$ on maps carrying the marked edges of $X$ to equivalences: a marked edge in $X\times(\Delta^n)^\flat$ has constant second coordinate and is tested at a parameter vertex. Hence it is a quasicategory by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. That same node's pointwise equivalence criterion identifies its core with $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,C^\natural)$. Indeed a sharp-parameter map has equivalence components by evaluating at every vertex of $X$. Conversely, if these components are equivalences, any marked product edge is the diagonal of the two triangles splitting it into a horizontal marked edge and a vertical equivalence edge; their images are composites of equivalences. Composition and its inverse witnesses are supplied by [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine]. This checks every product marking, not only vertexwise vertical edges. In degree $n$, membership in the core requires each parameter edge of the simplex to be an equivalence transformation; the pointwise criterion tests every such edge at each vertex of $X$, and the preceding product triangle then tests every required diagonal marking. The core is Kan by the cited functor-cone calculus.

source.place: Remark 3.1.3.1 at a point; Proposition 1.2.7.3; full-subcategory and pointwise marking identification.

proof.text:
For $0<k\leq n$ the fully marked horn $(\Lambda_k^n)^\sharp	o(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ is marked anodyne. For $n\geq3$ every edge is already in the horn, so it is the pushout of (i) or (ii) adding the source markings. For $n=2$, first fill the underlying horn with (i) or (ii), retaining all old markings; the only new edge is then marked using (iii) if $k=1$, and [lem-coef-marked-triangle-cancellation] if $k=2$. For $n=1,k=1$, use (ii). Let $j:X	o Y$ be any degreewise injective marked map. A lifting square for a positive-index horn against $r:\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(Y,C^
atural)	o\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,C^
atural)$ adjoints to a map from the domain of $j\square((\Lambda_k^n)^\sharp	o(\Delta^n)^\sharp)$ into $C^
atural$. Steps 6-9 make this map marked anodyne (interchange the two factors), and Step 1 gives its filler. Thus $r$ is a right fibration. Its target is Kan by Step 10, so [lem-cbc-right-fibration-space-fiber] makes $r$ a Kan fibration.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.3.6; sharp right-horn attachments and the right-hand version of Lemma 2.1.3.3.

proof.text: If $j$ is marked anodyne, a boundary lifting square for the same $r$ adjoints to lifting $C^\natural\to*$ against $j\square((\partial\Delta^n)^\sharp\to(\Delta^n)^\sharp)$. The latter is marked anodyne by Steps 6-9. Step 1 supplies the filler, for every $n\geq0$, with $n=0$ giving extension of vertices. Thus $r$ is a trivial Kan fibration, using exactly the boundary-lifting characterization of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper].

source.place: Remark 3.1.3.4, with the boundary adjunction written explicitly.

proof.text: Finally consider the finite detector $A$. In any map $A\to C$, the face equations in the statement identify the vertices of $\sigma$ as $(y,x,y,x)$. Its edges $[0,1]$ and $[2,3]$ are both $e$, while $[0,2]$ and $[1,3]$ are the respective identities. Put $g=\sigma|_{[1,2]}$. The faces on $[0,1,2]$ and $[1,2,3]$ are the inverse-triangle witnesses $ge=\mathrm{id}_y$ and $eg=\mathrm{id}_x$. Thus the newly marked edge $[0,1]$ is already an equivalence under every such map. Now take any $n$-simplex of $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(A^\flat,C^\natural)$. At each parameter vertex the preceding calculation makes the image of this edge an equivalence. Its product with any parameter edge is a diagonal whose two coordinate edges are equivalences (the vertical edge is already marked in $A^\flat\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp$). Their composite is an equivalence by the composition and inverse homotopies of [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine]. Consequently the map preserves the extra markings of $A\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp$ automatically. Restriction is therefore a degreewise bijection with the same faces and degeneracies, hence an isomorphism of simplicial sets. It is a trivial Kan fibration by the boundary characterization in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper].

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.7(1), the finite detector; the inverse triangles and parameter marking check are explicit.

proof.text: The constructions in the preceding steps are universe-relative. Countable filler sequences, the well-orderings of small sets of edges and simplices, representatives of countable objects, and the $\aleph_1$-stage small-object construction all belong to the input universe. Horns and the finite detector are finite. Products, pushouts, their degreewise markings and the mapping simplicial sets between fixed small objects are small there. No testing against a larger collection of objects was needed in any lifting argument. In particular the functorial replacement of Step 3 stays in the input universe.

proof_origin.place: Expanded point-case argument of Sections 3.1.1-3.1.3, read online. Not archived under literature/; WANTED in report.md. The proof explicitly handles saturation, all eight products, mapping adjunctions and the finite detector.
